Introduction

Whether it’s rolling the dice, reading your weekly horoscope, or running the numbers, it’s no secret that we are constantly weighing the outcomes of each decision we make and trying to place them in our favor. The end result, however, tends to not always go as we originally expected. We are studying correlation or trends that we see for each outcome. Say historically, if I study engineering, I am likely to end up with a stable career based on previous trends related to engineering. This is where Applied Statistics offers a helping hand. Applied Statistics is designed to help you find the probability that you will reach the end goal you want or land within the range of numbers that you expect. So, this begs the question: How likely are you to…

  1. End up in that career that you’ve always wanted
  2. Afford that nice home with a view that you’ve always wanted
  3. Buy that new car that flew past you on the highway

This page allows you the opportunity to explore the different factors that could impact large scale decisions such as these.

Episode 1: Living In New York City: How Likely Is It?

Whether it’s your fear of the subway or the unpredictable weather of New York City, it is undeniably the most perfect place for a young person to start their life. During my brief visit to New York City, I can tell you that if you’re a directionally challenged person, you’re screwed without any help. I had to spend thirty minutes hunting down the shop my family was at before I found it and I couldn’t quite figure out why. I just couldn’t find the spot. But as I spent time circling the space for that time, one thing was very apparent: New York City is designed for your twenties. I saw college and grad students everywhere I turned but I kept asking myself, how possible is it to live in a place like this? A space so packed and so commercialized has to be almost impossible to live in, yet every movie on the planet has depicted an entry-level role in the city as a common thing. The following scenario is meant to put this theory into a practical test. Note that it says Person B below, but treat them much like you treated the tooth fairy after age 10: a figment of your imagination.

Person B: Person B has been saving up for the last five years to rent and work in New York City. Given the amount in his savings: $10,000, how likely is he to be able to live in New York City for his two year training program with an investment company?

My first thought was that this scenario felt too general. There are too many factors to consider when it comes to living in such a vast, diverse city. After further analysis, however, there are some averages across cost of living and rent prices that can be applied across the board. It is vital, however, to note that this exercise assumes that there would be fixed rent and food prices, which tends to not be the case in the real world. The following averages were gathered about the average person’s cost of living in New York City:

  • Rent: $5,245
  • Utilities: $260.4, $203.89
  • Transportation: $132
  • Food: $90.71
  • Healthcare: $527.54
  • Miscellaneous: $87.1
  • Income: $79,713

To measure the likelihood that Person B would be able to live in New York City for the two-year time frame was tested through a simulation called Monte Carlo. This basically means that the computer ran these numbers and generated an average amount of money left, taking into account the initial savings but then that estimate was updated repeatedly as each simulation ran. The result to this is as follows:

  • The likelihood that this person would be bankrupt and not be able to live in the city AT ALL: 0% (lets goooooo)
  • The total savings they’ll have after their time there: $12,306.64
  • Will this person be able to make this experience work? Yes

Episode 3: Cost Of Living Analysis (Houston, TX)

Studies Show has mostly looked at the likelihood of a move, a career switch, or a major life transition, but what would it actually look like in practice? What would it look like for the different costs of living to evolve over time? That is what I aim to answer with the following scenario:

Person AA: Person AA has been a pre-med student for four years. As a student at Notre Dame, she entered undergrad with the hope of one day entering her dream role of being a dermatologist. This dream, however, was short-lived as she realized how lengthy the process would take to get there. She did, however, know that she wanted to move back to Houston, Texas to take care of her mom and start her career there. The question now is, what does this look like realistically? Given the provided assumptions and what is known about cost of living in Houston, Texas, how will Person AA’s cost of living evolve over time?

I will admit. This scenario proved harder to solve than originally planned because there were a vast amount of factors to account for, such as groceries, changing transportation expenses, and rent prices. To see what this would look like in the long-term, I decided to walk a mile in Person AA’s shoes and see what this transition would practically look like, starting with choosing a starting career:

I first looked at the most popular industries in the area to ensure her best chance of success. Given that Person AA was originally pre-med, I decided she would thrive in an adjacent role: Healthcare administration. This brought her monthly budget to roughly $10,794. I then calculated a monthly budget for Person AA using median rates for cost of living expenses in Houston, Texas, such as groceries, transportation, and miscellaneous expenses:

Car loan payment$3,000
Transportation (gas/insurance/maintenance)$430
Healthcare$97.20
Groceries$196.40
Miscellaneous$208.97
School loan payment$1,000
Emergency fund$1,000
Total expenses$5,932.57
Remaining for rent$4,861.43

As you can see from the table, Houston, Texas was proven to be one of the most comfortable places to transition to. Even after all monthly expenses, including two with an interest rate, moving to the Houston metropolitan area is still very doable.

Next, I looked at median rent prices in each major neighborhood in Houston, Texas.

As you can see, even with her high monthly expenses, she still has plenty left over for rent. So, in terms of where she should live, I decided on a 2 bedroom apartment that would comfortably fit her and her mother. Given this information, I then constructed the following graph:

Her monthly savings begin to skyrocket as her student loans and car loans drop significantly. Which brings about the question, what then? Given that Person AA has not graduated for long, I recommend that they take advantage of these higher savings and either apply them to a Roth IRA or assist their mother in paying down the medical expenses. Lastly, I encourage Person AA to feed into their emergency fund to account for the possibility of layoffs or other major healthcare costs.

Important Caveats & Limitations

This scenario was constructed on the assumption of fixed cost of living expenses, such as groceries, gas prices, and transportation. It also assumes that Person AA’s mother is able to use some of her retirement fund in order to pay off any medical bills while staying with Person AA, and lastly, the graph assumes that Person AA has a steady career growth and will naturally transition from a healthcare administrator, to a data scientist, and then a management consultant.

Citations

Sources: Cost of Living Comparison | Houston.org; Rental Market Trends & Average Rent in Houston, TX | Rent.; AAA Fuel Prices; Claude AI; Levels.fyi: Security Analyst, Greater Houston Area.

Episode 5: Paying Off Medical Debt

It is no secret that living in a major city is an incredibly costly endeavor. Whether you are just moving in or have been there your whole life, the tradeoff of living in a walkable city is definitely the huge hit to your bank account. Add on top of that a medical debt, which can happen to any healthy or unhealthy adult at any time and watch how that changes your monthly budget. That is what I hope to demonstrate with the following scenario:

Person 2B: Person 2B was recently in a car accident along with his friend. He is in his mid thirties and living alone while his friend is in his mid-twenties and just beginning his career in accounting. They had also run into a car of two people that were both impacted by the accident; one of them is a well-off investment banker and the other is a social worker. Given that the accident mostly impacted Person 2B and his friend, while smaller injuries were sustained to the two passengers in the other vehicle, how long will each member in the crash take to recover from the medical expenses?

To demonstrate this, it is important to first look at the debt of each member of the accident. Person 2B sustained a total of 120K worth of injuries and his friend 110K. Person 3 (our investment banker) sustained 50K of injuries while his friend, Person 4, sustained 40K of injuries. Given their debts and their respective lifestyles, I calculated how much each person can contribute to their medical expenses each month:

For further context, I have provided the following table:

PersonTotal DebtMonthly PaymentPayment as % of Monthly SalaryMonths to Pay OffTime to Pay Off
Person 2B$120,000$3,00040%403 yr 4 mo
Person 2$110,000$1,50030%73.3 (74 payments)6 yr 2 mo
Person 3$50,000$10,00040%55 mo
Person 4$40,000$1,00022%403 yr 4 mo

As you can see, the financial situation of a person deeply impacts how they recover from these injuries and what the next several years of their life will look like in some situations. This is not to say that everyone should pigeon hole themselves into careers that do not suit them in case this ever happens, but stresses the importance of an emergency fund early on in life as well as ensuring that you are staying within your budget. Because although each person had the means to contribute to their debt each month, they didn’t all contribute the same proportions. Person 2 and 4 contributed smaller portions because they had tied up larger debts in miscellaneous expenses as well as car and health insurance compared to the others.

Important Caveats & Limitations

Please note that this scenario operates on the following assumptions:

  1. The following expenses will stay the same: Rent & Utilities, transportation, groceries, and internet
  2. The following expenses will decrease: miscellaneous
  3. The following expenses will increase or stay the same: emergency fund/savings and salary, health insurance, and car insurance
  4. There will not be another hefty medical expense in the near future, such as from an operation

This scenario also assumed that no one was at fault for the accident and had to pay an additional expense to an insurance company.

Citations

Sources: Salary.com: Cost of Living in Seattle, WA; Claude AI.

Episode 2: Running The Boston Marathon: How Likely Is It?

It truly is a cannon event to pick up running in your twenties. My for you page has flooded me with run clubs, workout content, pilates girlies, you name it. The thought of a marathon seems so intimidating to the average person and it is. I mean, genuinely, why on earth would you put your body through such a feat when your life is hard enough as is? Much for the same reason we do pretty much anything: ……………….attention. So say you want peak attention, like Person C, how likely are you to qualify for the Boston Marathon given the following scenario:

Person C: Person C has been exhausted trying to train for a marathon. She has the following times and distances after roughly three months of training. Given this training, how likely is she to qualify for the Boston Marathon in three months time?

  • Mile time: 6:45 min
  • Half Marathon: 3hr 5mins (pretty solid, honestly)
  • Practice 20 miler: 4hrs 50 mins (yes, people actually do this)

(And three months of truly locking in.) The following information was collected on Boston Qualifier times:

  • Mile time: 7:30 min
  • Half Marathon: 1hr 35mins - 1hr 45mins
  • Practice 20 miler: 2hr 30 mins - 3 hrs
  • Average training time frame: 3 - 4 months

A Monte Carlo simulation was run 1000 times to estimate the times this person would have after 3 months. This means that the computer estimated the time for the Boston Marathon and then updated it after running the simulation more and more times. The following marathon time was calculated: 6 hours, 4 mins, 43 seconds.

The Boston Qualifier time for both men and women is between 3 hours to 4 hours. So unfortunately, yes, you can run a marathon. Yes, you will have the attention, but no, unfortunately you will not be Usain Bolt in that three month time frame (you’re doing amazing, sweetie).

Episode 4: Quit Doomscrolling: How Likely Is It?

I once had to cram for an exam in college and decided it was the perfect day to look away from my phone. I locked myself in a basement of a library, put my phone on my back, and started speed writing on my study sheet. Halfway through the study session, unconsciously, I started “scrolling” on the table as if my phone was there and as if Instagram was opened right in front of me. This unconscious act inspired the following scenario to see if an average person could cut back on this habit and under extreme cases, quit the habit altogether. My day in the library showed me that although doomscrolling cannot be stopped in a day, maybe it’s possible to cut back on it and its effects on my health.

Person G: Person G is a typical college student that has decided to cut back on doomscrolling because they noticed they are having trouble sleeping and completing their school work. They have decided to set the noble goal of cutting back doomscrolling to just one hour a day. This includes doomscrolling both on Instagram and TikTok. They decided to do this before their final exam season, which is in roughly 50 days. How long will it take them to cut back from four hours of doomscrolling to just one hour a day?

This scenario first made me look into the effects of doomscrolling on mental health in the forms of depression, anxiety, insomnia, etc. So I looked at a study conducted on Chinese college students to see how strong these correlations are. The study found that although there isn’t clear causation between doomscrolling and mental health, there are multiple statistically significant correlations between them. So, if doomscrolling creates a loop of being more receptive to negative news, losing sleep, and worsening depression, how can you cut back on it and all of its side effects? I decided to research this by looking at the following factors:

US National AveragePerson G’s Average
Sleep per night6.7 hours/night5 hours/night
Caffeine consumption159 mg/day120 mg/day
Credit hours12-1515
Enrollment intensityFull time (most often)Full time
Daily screen time7 hours8 hours per day
Social media time2+ hours per day4 hours per day
Average stress levelModerate stressHigh stress
Cut back amount4-5 minutes of doomscrolling per day3 minutes per day

Despite my research looking at Chinese college students, these factors will look at the averages across American college students. As you can see, Person G has higher stress and worse habits than the average college student. These worse baselines are going to make the 50 day goal even harder. Based on the average college student’s habits, they would be able to cut back 4-5 minutes of doomscrolling a day, but since Person G (they’re trying their best, I swear) has worse baselines, they will be able to cut back 3 minutes of doomscrolling per day.

Results: After conducting analysis in R, it will take Person G 89.92 days to cut back from 4 hours of doomscrolling a day to just one hour. They will not be able to reach this goal by the time their finals roll around, however, this is not meant to discourage them. Just because they can’t cut back dramatically in that time frame, it doesn’t mean it’s not worth the effort to fix this habit.
